q_0001.stem: A community health nurse is determining whether a family of four is financially eligible for Medicaid and CHIP. Which federal measure applies?
options: Poverty thresholds issued by the US Bureau of the Census
Federal Poverty Guidelines issued by USDHHS
The Supplemental Poverty Measure
The Consumer Price Index
q_0001.rationale: The Federal Poverty Guidelines are issued every year by USDHHS and determine whether a person or family is financially eligible for assistance programs, including marketplace insurance savings, Medicaid, and CHIP.
q_0001.trap: Thresholds are the Census Bureau's product and exist primarily for statistical purposes. Sort it by what the question is doing: eligibility for a program means guideline; reporting a statistic means threshold.

q_0002.stem: Poverty thresholds are issued by which body, and used primarily for what?
options: USDHHS, to determine program eligibility
US Bureau of the Census, primarily for statistical purposes
USDA, to set SNAP benefit levels
Bureau of Labor Statistics, to calculate the Consumer Price Index
q_0002.rationale: Poverty thresholds come from the US Bureau of the Census and are used primarily for statistical purposes.
q_0002.trap: This is the mirror image of the eligibility question. The two federal terms are the single most testable pair in this section, and they are easiest to invert when the stem names an agency rather than a use.

q_0003.stem: The Federal Poverty Guidelines are updated annually to stay consistent with which measure?
options: The Supplemental Poverty Measure
Median household income
The Consumer Price Index
The federal minimum wage
q_0003.rationale: The Consumer Price Index measures change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services, and the guidelines are updated each year to stay consistent with it.

q_0004.stem: Under the 2020 Poverty Guidelines for the 48 contiguous states and DC, what is the guideline for a family of four?
q_0004.rationale: The 2020 guideline is $12,760 for one person and $26,200 for a family of four.

q_0005.stem: In the 2020 Poverty Guidelines table for the 48 contiguous states and DC, how much does the guideline increase for each additional person at every step from a family of one through a family of eight?
options: It does not increase by a fixed amount
q_0005.rationale: The table's own increments are $4,480 per person at every step from 1 through 8.
q_0005.trap: The textbook prints "add $5,600 per person," but that line applies only to units of eight or more and appears to be an error carried over from the Alaska schedule. Do not state $5,600 as the general per-person rule. The safe phrasing is "$12,760 for one person, $26,200 for a family of four; higher for Alaska and Hawaii."

q_0006.stem: Which statements about the Supplemental Poverty Measure are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It is reported by the Census Bureau
Its thresholds vary by geographic area
Its thresholds vary by homeownership status
It replaced the Federal Poverty Guidelines for determining program eligibility
Its thresholds can be higher than those of the official measure
q_0006.rationale: The Census also reports the Supplemental Poverty Measure, whose thresholds vary by geographic area and homeownership status and can be higher than the official measure.
q_0006.trap: The SPM is an additional statistical measure, not an eligibility instrument. Eligibility still runs through the USDHHS guidelines.

q_0007.stem: What was the official US poverty rate in 2018, and what was notable about it?
options: 9.7%, the first increase in a decade
11.8%, the fourth consecutive annual decline
16.2%, unchanged from the previous year
12.9%, the fourth consecutive annual increase
q_0007.rationale: The 2018 official poverty rate was 11.8%, the fourth consecutive annual decline. It was expected to rise beginning in 2020 because of COVID-19.

q_0008.stem: Which statements about child poverty in the US in 2018 are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The poverty rate for children under 18 was 16.2%
Nearly 1 in 6 children lived in poverty
Approximately 11.9 million children lived in poverty
The oldest children are the poorest
Nearly 73% of poor children in America are children of color
q_0008.rationale: In 2018 the rate for children under 18 was 16.2% — nearly 1 in 6, approximately 11.9 million children — and nearly 73% of poor children in America are children of color. Children are the poorest age group in America.
q_0008.trap: It is the youngest children who are the poorest, not the oldest. Also note Chapter 23 reports 17% for children 0–17 in 2017; different years, both in the assigned reading, so match the figure to the year in the stem.

q_0009.stem: Which statements about poverty among adults 65 and older are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The 2018 rate was 9.7%
The rate decreases with advancing age
The rate is higher among women
The rate is higher among African Americans and Hispanics
Under the official measure in 2017, 4.7 million adults 65+ lived in poverty
q_0009.rationale: The 2018 rate for adults 65+ was 9.7%; the rate increases with age and is higher among women, African Americans, and Hispanics. Under the official measure, 4.7 million adults 65+ lived in poverty in 2017.
q_0009.trap: The rate rises with age rather than falling — an easy inversion when the rest of the stem is otherwise familiar.

q_0010.stem: Among full-time, year-round employed workers, women earn approximately how much per dollar earned by a man?
q_0010.rationale: Full-time year-round employed women earn $0.82 per $1.00 a man earns. Median 2018 earnings for full-time work were $55,291 for men and $45,097 for women. The 2018 poverty rate was 12.9% for women, down from 13.6% in 2017, versus 10.6% for men.

q_0011.stem: Which terms does the chapter use to describe types of poverty? Select all that apply.
options: Persistent poverty
Neighborhood poverty
Crisis poverty
Multigenerational poverty
q_0011.rationale: The chapter states that persistent poverty and neighborhood poverty are used to describe types of poverty, and adds multigenerational poverty.
q_0011.trap: Crisis poverty appears only in the homelessness section, as a synonym for transitional homelessness. Presenting all four as a set of "poverty types" is a defensible synthesis but is not how the book frames it — if the question asks what the book calls types of poverty, leave crisis poverty out.

q_0012.stem: Which term describes individuals and families who remain poor for long periods and pass poverty on to their descendants?
options: Neighborhood poverty
Persistent poverty
Multigenerational poverty
Crisis poverty
q_0012.rationale: Persistent poverty is defined as remaining poor for long periods and passing poverty on to descendants.
q_0012.trap: Multigenerational poverty is the near-neighbor here. The book anchors multigenerational poverty to specific named populations rather than to the mechanism of transmission.

q_0013.stem: Which term describes geographically defined areas of high poverty characterized by dilapidated housing and high levels of unemployment?
options: Persistent poverty
Multigenerational poverty
Neighborhood poverty
Transitional poverty
q_0013.rationale: Neighborhood poverty is defined by geography — high-poverty areas marked by dilapidated housing and high unemployment.

q_0014.stem: Multigenerational poverty is described as common among which populations? Select all that apply.
options: African Americans in the South
Hispanics along the border of Mexico
American Indians who live in states with multiple reservations
Recent immigrants in coastal metropolitan areas
q_0014.rationale: The chapter names three populations: African Americans in the South, Hispanics along the Mexican border, and American Indians living in states with multiple reservations.
q_0014.trap: There are three named populations, not two. Guide v1's figure lists only the first two while its own drill page lists all three — the third is the one that gets dropped.

q_0015.stem: Which statements about toxic stress in children living in poverty are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: It involves prolonged activation of cortisol, norepinephrine, and adrenaline
It involves inflammatory mediators such as cytokines
Much of the lifelong increased risk of cardiovascular and metabolic disease traces to it
It is mitigated by stable, supportive relationships with adults in early childhood
It resolves spontaneously once the child reaches school age
q_0015.rationale: Toxic stress is prolonged activation of stress hormones and inflammatory mediators in children living in poverty; much of the lifelong cardiovascular and metabolic risk traces to it, and stable supportive adult relationships in early childhood mitigate it.

q_0016.stem: The fact bank names breastfeeding as a mitigator of toxic stress. By what stated mechanism?
options: Skin-to-skin contact raises maternal oxytocin and prolactin, decreases cortisol, and reduces infant allostatic load
Breast milk antibodies directly suppress cytokine production in the infant
Breastfeeding lowers the infant's caloric requirement during stress
Breastfeeding delays the onset of the infant's own stress response until after infancy
q_0016.rationale: Skin-to-skin contact raises maternal oxytocin and prolactin, decreases cortisol, and reduces infant allostatic load.

q_0017.stem: According to Box 25.1, which are effects of poverty on the health of children? Select all that apply.
options: Higher rates of prematurity, low birth weight, and birth defects
Elevated blood lead levels
Iron-deficiency anemia
Increased risk for homelessness
Increased opportunities for education, income, and occupation
q_0017.rationale: Box 25.1 lists higher rates of prematurity, low birth weight and birth defects, higher infant mortality, increased chronic disease, increased traumatic death and injury, nutritional deficits, growth restriction and developmental delays, iron-deficiency anemia, elevated blood lead levels, infections, increased risk for homelessness, and decreased opportunities for education, income, and occupation.
q_0017.trap: Opportunities for education, income, and occupation decrease, not increase. ---

q_0018.stem: How does HUD define a homeless person?
options: A person with no permanent mailing address
A person who lacks a fixed, regular, and adequate nighttime residence
A person living below the federal poverty guideline without housing assistance
A person who has spent at least 30 consecutive nights in an emergency shelter
q_0018.rationale: HUD's definition is "a person who lacks a fixed, regular, and adequate nighttime residence."

q_0019.stem: A 46-year-old man has experienced homelessness five separate times over the past three years, totaling about 14 months. He has no documented disabling condition. How is his homelessness best classified?
options: Chronic, because he meets the frequency and duration criteria
Episodic, because he moves in and out of homelessness
Transitional, because each episode was brief
Chronic, because any homelessness exceeding 12 months is chronic
q_0019.rationale: Chronic homelessness requires a disability AND either four or more episodes in three years totaling at least 12 months, or continuous homelessness for one year. Without the disability, the time criterion alone does not make it chronic. Moving in and out of homelessness is episodic.
q_0019.trap: This is the single most reliable distractor in the homelessness section — a scenario that satisfies the time criterion but omits the disability. Both elements are required.

q_0020.stem: Which category accounts for the majority of homelessness over time?
options: Chronic homelessness
Episodic homelessness
Transitional homelessness
Veteran homelessness
q_0020.rationale: Transitional homelessness — typically caused by a catastrophic event leading to a short shelter stay and eventual transition to permanent housing — accounts for the majority of homelessness over time.
q_0020.trap: Chronic homelessness is the intuitive but wrong answer, because it is the most visible and most discussed category. The inversion is easy and it is worth over-learning in this direction.

q_0021.stem: Transitional homelessness is also known by which other name?
options: Episodic poverty
Crisis poverty
Situational poverty
Neighborhood poverty
q_0021.rationale: Transitional homelessness is also called crisis poverty, and it is the only place the term crisis poverty appears in the chapter.

q_0022.stem: Which features characterize episodic homelessness? Select all that apply.
options: Moving in and out of homelessness
Marked by hardship and struggle, including chronic unemployment
A younger population
Frequently associated with mental health and substance abuse problems
Typically resolves into permanent housing after a single short shelter stay
q_0022.rationale: Episodic homelessness means moving in and out of homelessness, marked by hardship and struggle including chronic unemployment, in a younger population often with mental health and substance abuse problems.
q_0022.trap: Resolving into permanent housing after one short stay describes transitional homelessness.

q_0023.stem: On a single night in 2019, approximately how many people in the US experienced homelessness, and what proportion were sheltered?
options: About 568,000, with 63% sheltered and 37% unsheltered
About 568,000, with 37% sheltered and 63% unsheltered
About 328,000, with 63% sheltered and 37% unsheltered
About 1.2 million, with half sheltered
q_0023.rationale: The 2019 point-in-time count found approximately 568,000 people experiencing homelessness, 63% sheltered in emergency shelters or transitional housing and 37% unsheltered — on the street, in abandoned buildings, or in other places not suitable for human habitation.
q_0023.trap: The sheltered/unsheltered split is easy to reverse. The majority are sheltered.

q_0024.stem: In the 2019 point-in-time count, which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: 27% were under age 25
8% were veterans
African Americans remain consistently overrepresented
Homelessness increased 3% in West Coast states from 2018 to 2019
In several states, at least 95% of the homeless population was unsheltered
q_0024.rationale: 27% were under 25 and 8% were veterans; African Americans remain consistently overrepresented; homelessness rose 3% in West Coast states between 2018 and 2019, likely due to the moderate climate.
q_0024.trap: In Maine, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New York, and North Dakota at least 95% of the homeless population was sheltered, not unsheltered.

q_0025.stem: Why do point-in-time counts undercount homelessness? Select all that apply.
options: HUD's definition excludes families doubled up with friends or family
Some people live in motels, vehicles, or hidden locations and never contact service agencies
Some people refuse to be interviewed
Rural homelessness is less apparent because people are hidden from sight
Counts are conducted only in states that opt in
q_0025.rationale: The National Coalition for the Homeless notes that HUD's definition excludes doubled-up families, that many people live in motels, vehicles, or hidden locations and never interact with counting volunteers, and that some refuse interview. Rural homelessness is hidden — in woods in tents or campers, in barns or ice sheds, or on a friend's couch.

q_0026.stem: The chapter attributes respiratory conditions and tuberculosis among people experiencing homelessness primarily to which cause?
options: Untreated chronic disease
Crowded sleeping conditions
Exposure to cold outdoor air
High-sodium shelter and fast food
q_0026.rationale: Respiratory conditions and TB are attributed to crowded sleeping conditions.
q_0026.trap: Each health problem in this section carries its own stated cause, and the causes are interchangeable-looking. Learn them as pairs rather than as a list of conditions.

q_0027.stem: Why are peripheral vascular disease and hypertension common among people experiencing homelessness, according to the chapter?
options: Because they may be on their feet for long hours daily
Because of crowded sleeping conditions
Because of infestations and poor skin integrity
Because of untreated diabetes
q_0027.rationale: The chapter attributes peripheral vascular disease and hypertension to being on their feet for long hours daily.

q_0028.stem: The chapter attributes diabetes and nutritional deficits in this population to which cause?
options: Being on their feet for long hours daily
Shelter and fast food being high in sodium
Crowded sleeping conditions
Hypothermia and heat-related illness
q_0028.rationale: Diabetes and nutritional deficits are attributed to shelter and fast food being high in sodium.

q_0029.stem: Which barriers to care are named for people experiencing homelessness? Select all that apply.
options: Not knowing where to get treated
Lack of transportation and lack of identification
Embarrassment and self-consciousness about appearance and hygiene
Nervousness or inability to fill out forms and answer questions
Statutory exclusion from emergency department care
q_0029.rationale: The named barriers are not knowing where to get treated, lack of transportation, lack of identification, embarrassment, nervousness or inability to complete forms and answer questions, and self-consciousness about appearance and hygiene. Care is usually crisis-oriented and sought in emergency departments.

q_0030.stem: Which statement best captures the chapter's characterization of health promotion for people experiencing homelessness?
options: Health promotion is the primary focus of shelter-based nursing care
Health promotion is a luxury, not part of daily life
Health promotion is delivered mainly through emergency departments
Health promotion is mandated for all federally funded shelters
q_0030.rationale: The chapter states directly that health promotion is a luxury, not part of daily life. Care is crisis-oriented and sought in emergency departments.

q_0031.stem: Conditions such as TB and HIV/AIDS are described as extremely difficult to treat or control in this population for what stated reason?
options: They require regular uninterrupted treatment, which is not possible without adequate housing
They are excluded from emergency department protocols
Shelter policies prohibit storing medications on site
They are rarely diagnosed before end-stage disease
q_0031.rationale: Conditions needing regular uninterrupted treatment, such as TB and HIV/AIDS, are extremely difficult to treat or control without adequate housing.

q_0032.stem: Approximately what proportion of unaccompanied homeless youth are estimated to be LGBTQ?
q_0032.rationale: An estimated 40% of unaccompanied homeless youth are LGBTQ.

q_0033.stem: Which findings are described among homeless adolescents? Select all that apply.
options: Earlier onset of sexual activity
Poorer health status and decreased access to care
High risk for AIDS and hepatitis B
Exchanging sex for food, clothing, and shelter, placing girls at high risk for unintended pregnancy
Lower rates of runaway behavior than housed peers
q_0033.rationale: Homeless adolescents show earlier onset of sexual activity, poorer health status, decreased access to care, and high risk for AIDS and hepatitis B. Many exchange sex for food, clothing, and shelter. Histories of runaway behavior, physical abuse, and sexual abuse are common — more, not less, than among housed peers.

q_0034.stem: Which statements about homeless veterans are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: On a single night in January 2019, 37,085 veterans were homeless
Numbers have dropped nearly 50% since 2009
About 50% have serious mental illness
About 70% have substance use issues
The majority are part of a family unit
q_0034.rationale: On a single night in January 2019, 37,085 veterans were homeless; only 2% were part of a family; 90.3% were men and 8.9% women. Numbers dropped nearly 50% since 2009, credited to HUD-VASH, SSVF, and coordinated VA/HUD effort. About 50% have serious mental illness and 70% have substance use issues.
q_0034.trap: Only 2% were part of a family — the majority are unmarried and may be socially isolated.

q_0035.stem: Approximately what proportion of homeless persons has a severe mental illness?
options: One in ten
One in five
One in three
One in two
q_0035.rationale: One in five homeless persons has a severe mental illness, with similar rates of chronic substance abuse. Both are often associated with chronic homelessness.

q_0036.stem: Which characteristics are described among pregnant women experiencing homelessness? Select all that apply.
options: Younger, unmarried, uninsured, and less educated
Less likely to initiate and sustain breastfeeding
Fewer prenatal and well-child visits
Higher rates of STIs, addiction, and kidney and bladder infections
Birth outcomes comparable to housed women of the same age
q_0036.rationale: Homeless pregnant women are at high risk for complex health problems — younger, unmarried, uninsured, less educated, less likely to breastfeed, with fewer prenatal and well-child visits, higher rates of STIs and addiction, poorer nutritional status, more kidney and bladder infections, and poorer birth outcomes including lower birth weight and preterm labor. ---

q_0037.stem: Danawi et al. (2016) identify four social determinants of health that influence teen pregnancy rates. Which are they? Select all that apply.
options: Income
Education
Social support networks
Living environment
Access to abortion services
q_0037.rationale: The four named social determinants are income, education, social support networks, and living environment.

q_0038.stem: On the 2019 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, what percentage of surveyed high school students were sexually active?
q_0038.rationale: The 2019 YRBS found 27.4% of surveyed high school students were sexually active.

q_0039.stem: The Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System monitors how many categories of health-risk behaviors?
options: Four
Five
Six
Eight
q_0039.rationale: The YRBS monitors six categories of health-risk behaviors, one of which is sexual behaviors related to unintended pregnancy and STDs including HIV.

q_0040.stem: According to Guttmacher (2019), what proportion of adolescents reported contraceptive use at first intercourse?
options: 91% of females and 77% of males
77% of females and 91% of males
65% of females and 84% of males
84% of both females and males
q_0040.rationale: 77% of females and 91% of males reported contraceptive use at first intercourse.
q_0040.trap: The two figures are easy to swap. The higher figure belongs to males.

q_0041.stem: What is meant by sexual debut?
options: First experience with intercourse
First romantic relationship
Onset of puberty
First use of contraception
q_0041.rationale: Sexual debut is the first experience with intercourse, and it has a significant impact on pregnancy risk.

q_0042.stem: How does the chapter describe peer reinforcement of teen parenting? Select all that apply.
options: Exaggerating the risks of birth control
Discouraging abortion and adoption
Glamorizing the impending birth
Teens are more likely to be sexually active if their friends are
Encouraging early entry into prenatal care
q_0042.rationale: Teens are more likely to be sexually active if their friends are, and peers reinforce teen parenting by exaggerating birth control risks, discouraging abortion and adoption, and glamorizing the impending birth.

q_0043.stem: A history of sexual victimization in adolescence is associated with which outcomes? Select all that apply.
options: Earlier initiation of voluntary intercourse
Being less likely to use birth control
Being more likely to use drugs or alcohol at first intercourse
Being more likely to have older partners
Delayed sexual debut
q_0043.rationale: A history of sexual abuse is associated with earlier initiation of voluntary intercourse, lower likelihood of birth control use, greater likelihood of drug or alcohol use at first intercourse, and older partners.
q_0043.trap: Every consequence runs toward earlier and higher-risk activity. A "delayed" option in this stem is always the distractor.

q_0044.stem: What does dual protection mean as the chapter uses the term?
options: Two hormonal contraceptives used together
A hormonal contraceptive, preferably LARC, plus a condom
A condom plus emergency contraception on hand
Contraception plus routine STI screening
q_0044.rationale: Dual protection is the use of a hormonal contraceptive, preferably LARC, plus a condom — the current recommendation for greatest protection against both pregnancy and STI.
q_0044.trap: The recommendation is specifically hormonal-plus-barrier. Two methods of the same kind is not dual protection, because the point is covering pregnancy and STI simultaneously.

q_0045.stem: Which methods are long-acting reversible contraception? Select all that apply.
options: Intrauterine devices
Contraceptive implants
Combined oral contraceptive pills
Depot injections given every three months
q_0045.rationale: LARC comprises IUDs and contraceptive implants. ACOG made a strong recommendation in 2012 to encourage adolescent use; LARC has the highest rates of continuation and of preventing pregnancy, rapid repeat pregnancy, and abortion in young women.

q_0046.stem: How does the chapter classify pregnant teenagers, and to what does it attribute their complications?
options: Average-risk patients; complications stem mainly from physiologic immaturity
High-risk obstetrical patients; complications can result from poverty, late entry into prenatal care, sporadic prenatal care, and limited self-care knowledge
High-risk obstetrical patients; complications stem almost entirely from inadequate nutrition
Average-risk patients provided prenatal care begins in the first trimester
q_0046.rationale: The chapter states plainly that pregnant teenagers are considered high-risk obstetrical patients, with complications resulting from poverty, late entry into prenatal care, sporadic prenatal care, and limited self-care knowledge.

q_0047.stem: A 16-year-old presents for her third prenatal visit. Regarding assessment for violence, which approach is correct?
options: Ask at the first prenatal visit, since a documented negative screen holds for the pregnancy
Ask at each visit, because frequent routine assessment is more revealing than a single inquiry
Ask only if the teen presents with unexplained injuries
Defer to social work, which screens at intake
q_0047.rationale: The nurse must ask about violence at each visit; frequent routine assessment is more revealing than a single inquiry at the first prenatal visit.
q_0047.trap: A single first-visit screen is the plausible-sounding distractor. Teens are more likely than adult women to experience violence during pregnancy, perpetrators include partners, family members, and acquaintances, and violence beginning in pregnancy may continue for years with increasing severity.

q_0048.stem: Which are named special issues in caring for the pregnant teen? Select all that apply.
options: Violence
Initiation of prenatal care
Low-birth-weight infants and preterm delivery
Nutrition, infant care, and repeat pregnancy
Schooling and educational needs
q_0048.rationale: The named issue areas are violence, initiation of prenatal care, low-birth-weight infants and preterm delivery, nutrition, infant care, repeat pregnancy, and schooling/educational needs.

q_0049.stem: What is the key nutritional consideration for a pregnant adolescent who is still growing?
options: Caloric needs match those of an adult pregnancy
She must increase caloric nutrients for her own growth as well as for the pregnancy
Caloric intake should be restricted to limit fetal size and ease delivery
Supplementation replaces the need for increased caloric intake
q_0049.rationale: The growing teen must increase caloric nutrients to meet her own growth needs as well as the pregnancy.

q_0050.stem: A 15-year-old has just received a positive pregnancy test. When is counseling about options most productive?
options: Immediately, while she is present and the result is fresh
At a follow-up visit, which is usually more productive than counseling at the time of initial results
Only after a parent or guardian has been notified
Only after the first prenatal visit with the obstetric provider
q_0050.rationale: A follow-up visit is usually more productive than counseling at the time of initial pregnancy testing results. Counseling should explore strengths and weaknesses, education and career plans, family finances, and personal values.
q_0050.trap: Counseling at the moment of the result feels efficient and responsive, but the chapter is explicit that the follow-up visit produces more.

q_0051.stem: Regarding abortion and adoption, what is the nurse's stated responsibility?
options: To recommend the option with the best health outcomes
To know local availability of services and refer appropriately for pregnancy counseling
To defer all discussion until the second trimester
To provide counseling personally rather than referring
q_0051.rationale: The nurse should know about local abortion and adoption services and refer appropriately. Affordable abortion services up to 13 weeks of gestation vary by community, and second-trimester services may require extensive travel and cost. For adoption, the teen needs information on current agency policies, including those allowing continued contact with the adopting family. ---

q_0052.stem: How does the chapter define mental health?
options: The absence of any diagnosable mental disorder
Being able to engage in productive activities, have fulfilling relationships, adapt to change, and cope with adversity
Stable mood and behavior maintained without treatment
Functioning within normal limits in family, school, or community activities
q_0052.rationale: Mental health is being able to engage in productive activities, have fulfilling relationships, adapt to change, and cope with adversity. It is an integral part of personal well-being, family and interpersonal relationships, and contribution to community.
q_0052.trap: Mental health and mental illness sit on a continuum; mental health is not defined as the absence of illness.

q_0053.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes mental disorders from mental illness?
options: They are interchangeable terms
Mental disorders are conditions marked by alterations in thinking, mood, or behavior associated with distress or impaired functioning; mental illness is collectively all diagnosable mental disorders
Mental illness refers only to conditions requiring hospitalization
Mental disorders are diagnosable; mental illness is a lay term with no clinical definition
q_0053.rationale: Mental disorders are conditions characterized by alterations in thinking, mood, or behavior associated with distress or impaired functioning. Mental illness is, collectively, all diagnosable mental disorders.

q_0054.stem: How does SAMHSA define any mental illness (AMI)?
options: Any mental, behavioral, or emotional disorder in the past year that met DSM-5 criteria
Any disorder causing serious functional impairment that substantially limits major life activities
Any disorder requiring psychotropic medication in the past year
Any disorder diagnosed before age 18
q_0054.rationale: AMI is defined as persons having any mental, behavioral, or emotional disorder in the past year that met DSM-5 criteria. In 2018 this was 47.6 million adults 18 and over.

q_0055.stem: How does SAMHSA define serious mental illness (SMI)?
options: Any mental, behavioral, or emotional disorder in the past year meeting DSM-5 criteria

Someone over 18 with a diagnosable mental, behavioral, or emotional disorder in the last year causing serious functional impairment that substantially interferes with or limits one or more major life activities
Any disorder requiring inpatient psychiatric admission in the last year
Any disorder present continuously for more than two years
q_0055.rationale: SMI applies to someone over 18 with a diagnosable disorder within the last year causing serious functional impairment that substantially interferes with or limits one or more major life activities. In 2018 this was 11.4 million adults.
q_0055.trap: AMI and SMI are separated by the functional impairment clause, not by diagnosis or by treatment setting. Formal diagnosis depends on a reduction in the person's ability to function as a result of the disorder.

q_0056.stem: What is the term for the under-18 parallel to serious mental illness?
options: Any mental illness
Childhood-onset mental disorder
Serious emotional disturbance
Developmental psychiatric disorder
q_0056.rationale: For people under 18, the parallel term is serious emotional disturbance, where the limitation is the ability to function in family, school, or community activities.

q_0057.stem: According to Healthy People 2030, approximately what proportion of people in the US will be diagnosed with a mental illness at some point in their lifetime?
options: About one quarter
About one third
About half
About two thirds
q_0057.rationale: Healthy People 2030 states that about half of all people in the US will be diagnosed with a mental illness at some point in their lifetime.

q_0058.stem: In 2018, SAMHSA reported how many adults 18 and over had both AMI and at least one substance use disorder?
options: 3.2 million
9.2 million
11.4 million
47.6 million
q_0058.rationale: 9.2 million adults had both AMI and at least one SUD; 3.2 million had co-occurring SMI and SUD; approximately 358,000 adolescents had a SUD and a major depressive episode.
q_0058.trap: 3.2 million is the SMI-plus-SUD figure and 11.4 million is SMI alone. The three numbers cluster and are easy to cross-assign.

q_0059.stem: WHO reports the combined global burden of mental health, substance abuse, and neurological disease at approximately what percentage?
q_0059.rationale: WHO reports the combined global burden at 14% and launched mhGAP, the mental health global action program. The WHO poster reads "No Health Without Mental Health."

q_0060.stem: What was the main reason for deinstitutionalization?
options: The discovery of psychotropic medications
Civil rights activism
The cost of institutional care
A federal court mandate to close state hospitals
q_0060.rationale: The main reason was the cost of institutional care. The discovery of psychotropic medications and civil rights activism were other influences.
q_0060.trap: Psychotropic medications and civil rights activism are both real contributors and both feel like better-sounding answers. The chapter names cost as the main reason and the other two as additional influences — hold that ranking.

q_0061.stem: What was the stated goal of deinstitutionalization?
options: To reduce the number of people carrying a psychiatric diagnosis
To improve quality of life by providing services in the communities where people lived rather than in large institutions
To transfer responsibility for psychiatric care from states to the federal government
To consolidate psychiatric care into regional centers of excellence
q_0061.rationale: The goal was to improve quality of life by delivering services in people's own communities rather than in large institutions. Community mental health centers were the intended destination for that care.

q_0062.stem: Which factors describe the failure of deinstitutionalization in implementation? Select all that apply.
options: Community-based services were not always in place when people were released
Continuity of care became a problem
Families were not prepared for the treatment responsibilities they assumed
Some people were placed in jails and prisons
Community mental health centers refused to accept discharged patients
q_0062.rationale: Community-based services were not always in place at release and continuity of care became a problem. Families assumed treatment responsibilities they were not prepared for, and few mental health systems offered education and support programs. Many were discharged to family, nursing homes, apartments, rooming houses, or single-room-occupancy hotels with little or no supervision, and some were placed in jails and prisons. Staff in nursing homes and personal care settings often lacked the skills to treat persons with mental disorders.

q_0063.stem: Which line does the chapter use to summarize deinstitutionalization?
options: "A solution in search of a problem"
"Noble in conception yet bankrupt in implementation"
"The right care in the wrong place"
"Community care without a community"
q_0063.rationale: The chapter's quotable line is "Deinstitutionalization was noble in conception yet bankrupt in implementation."

q_0064.stem: What did the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 mandate?
options: That community mental health centers receive federal block grants
That individuals with mental and physical disabilities not be discriminated against and be brought into the mainstream through access to employment and public services
That state psychiatric hospitals be closed within ten years
That insurers cover mental health at parity with physical health
q_0064.rationale: The ADA (1990) mandated that individuals with mental and physical disabilities not be discriminated against and be brought into the mainstream through access to employment and public services.

q_0065.stem: Suicide was the second leading cause of death for which age group?
options: Ages 5 to 14
Ages 10 to 24
Ages 15 to 34
Ages 18 to 25
q_0065.rationale: Suicide was the second leading cause of death for youth ages 10 to 24. Healthy People 2030 has objectives on reducing adolescent suicide attempts and screening for depression.

q_0066.stem: Which statement correctly describes the sex difference in youth suicide?
options: Females die by suicide about four times as often as males
Males die by suicide about four times as often as females, yet females are more likely to have suicidal thoughts
Males and females die by suicide at equal rates, but males report more suicidal thoughts
Females die by suicide more often and also report more suicidal thoughts
q_0066.rationale: Males die by suicide about four times as often as females, yet females are more likely to have suicidal thoughts.
q_0066.trap: The direction splits between completion and ideation. A question that reports both in the same direction is wrong regardless of which direction it picks.

q_0067.stem: Which environmental factors are named as putting children and adolescents at risk for disruption of normal development? Select all that apply.
options: Crowded living conditions
Violence
Separation from parents
Lack of consistent caregivers
Attendance at a large school
q_0067.rationale: Children and adolescents are at risk from biological, environmental, and psychosocial factors; the named environmental factors are crowded living conditions, violence, separation from parents, and lack of consistent caregivers. Exposure to community violence relates to significant stress and depression.

q_0068.stem: The chapter describes stigma in mental illness primarily as which phenomenon?
options: Reluctance of clinicians to document psychiatric diagnoses
Identifying people by the illness — "a schizophrenic" — rather than as a person with the illness
Insurance exclusion of psychiatric conditions
Underreporting of symptoms on population surveys
q_0068.rationale: People with mental illness are often identified by the illness rather than as a person with the illness.

q_0069.stem: Why does the onset of schizophrenia carry particular socioeconomic consequences?
options: It typically begins in later adulthood, after retirement savings are set
Onset often coincides with finishing schooling and starting a career, driving many into underemployment and poverty
It requires lifelong inpatient care in most cases
It disqualifies individuals from disability benefits
q_0069.rationale: Onset often coincides with finishing schooling and starting a career, driving many into underemployment, poverty, and lack of access to health services, housing, and social supports.

q_0070.stem: Low-income and minority groups face increased risk for mental illness largely because of what?
options: Higher underlying genetic vulnerability
Lack of access to services
Higher rates of misdiagnosis
Greater reluctance to accept treatment
q_0070.rationale: The chapter attributes increased risk in low-income and minority groups largely to lack of access to services. Cultural attitudes separately affect whether people seek mental health care, how they describe symptoms, duration of care, and outcomes. ---

q_0071.stem: What does the chapter say about sorting services for these high-risk groups into the three levels of prevention?
options: The three levels sort cleanly once the target population is identified
It is difficult to separate them, because interventions can be assigned to more than one level
Only primary and tertiary prevention apply to vulnerable populations
Secondary prevention is not applicable to homelessness
q_0071.rationale: The chapter states plainly that it is difficult to separate services for these high-risk groups into three levels because interventions can be assigned to more than one. Affordable housing may qualify as primary prevention but could also be an important secondary or tertiary intervention.
q_0071.trap: Expect a question that tests this ambiguity rather than clean sorting. If an item seems to demand one level for affordable housing, the chapter's own position is that it can sit in more than one.

q_0072.stem: Which interventions are named as primary prevention? Select all that apply.
options: Affordable housing and housing subsidies
Effective job-training programs and employer incentives
Birth control services and safe-sex education
Needle exchange programs and parent education
Helping enhance self-esteem in those already affected
q_0072.rationale: Primary prevention includes affordable housing, housing subsidies, effective job-training programs, employer incentives, preventive health care services, multisystem case management, birth control services, safe-sex education, needle exchange programs, parent education, and counseling programs.
q_0072.trap: Enhancing self-esteem in those already affected is the chapter's worked example of tertiary prevention.

q_0073.stem: A nurse targets persons on the verge of becoming high risk because of the threat of homelessness, as well as those who are newly homeless. This is an example of which level of prevention?
options: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
Quaternary
q_0073.rationale: This is the chapter's worked example of secondary prevention, which aims at reducing the prevalence or pathological nature of a condition through early diagnosis, prompt treatment, and limitation of disability.

q_0074.stem: A nurse works to enhance self-esteem among people already affected by homelessness and mental illness. This is an example of which level of prevention?
options: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
It cannot be classified
q_0074.rationale: This is the chapter's worked example of tertiary prevention, which reduces disability that has already resulted and restores function where possible.

q_0075.stem: A nurse provides education about stress reduction techniques to seniors attending a health fair. This is an example of which level of prevention?
options: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
Secondary, because the seniors are already at risk
q_0075.rationale: This is the chapter's worked example of primary prevention. The Levels of Prevention box for community mental health lists educating populations about mental health issues, teaching stress reduction techniques, supporting and providing prenatal education, and providing support to caregivers as primary prevention.

q_0076.stem: Using the chapter's own operating definition, which thresholds define "rural"?
options: Fewer than 50,000 residents or fewer than 10 persons per square mile
Fewer than 99 persons per square mile and communities of 20,000 or fewer inhabitants
Fewer than six persons per square mile
An urban core of at least 10,000 but fewer than 50,000 people
q_0076.rationale: The chapter's operating definition states rural refers to areas having fewer than 99 persons per square mile and communities having 20,000 or fewer inhabitants.
q_0076.trap: Box 24.1 phrases the same idea with "or" instead of "and." Both phrasings appear in the reading — the thresholds (20,000 and 99 per square mile) are what matter, not the conjunction. Don't get thrown by which connector a stem uses.

q_0077.stem: A region has fewer than six persons per square mile and schools more than 100 miles apart. Which classification best fits?
options: Rural
Frontier
Micropolitan
Non-core
q_0077.rationale: Frontier regions have fewer than six persons per square mile — a stricter threshold than rural's fewer-than-99. A stem describing extreme remoteness like widely spaced schools is cuing frontier, not just rural.
q_0077.trap: Frontier is easy to confuse with rural because both describe sparse areas. Rural is fewer than 99 per square mile; frontier is fewer than six.

q_0078.stem: A metropolitan area is defined by which population threshold for its core urban area?
options: 10,000 or more
20,000 or more
50,000 or more
99 or more per square mile
q_0078.rationale: A metropolitan area contains a core urban area of 50,000 or more population.
q_0078.trap: The chapter also defines "urban" elsewhere as cities with at least 20,000 but less than 50,000 residents. These are two different classification systems on the same page — metro/micro uses 50,000 and 10,000; urban-vs-rural uses 20,000 and 99 per square mile. Match the numbers to which system the stem is asking about.

q_0079.stem: Which population range defines a micropolitan area's urban core?
options: Fewer than 10,000
At least 10,000 but fewer than 50,000
At least 50,000
Exactly 20,000
q_0079.rationale: A micropolitan area contains an urban core of at least 10,000 but fewer than 50,000 people.
q_0079.trap: Non-core areas are defined as having no urban cluster of 10,000 or more — don't treat "non-core" as a general synonym for rural; it's a specific tier below micropolitan.

q_0080.stem: Which statements correctly distinguish farm residency from nonfarm residency? Select all that apply.
options: Farm residency is outside the area zoned as "city limits"
Nonfarm residency is within the area zoned as "city limits"
Farm residency usually infers involvement in agriculture
Nonfarm residency is another term for frontier living
q_0080.rationale: Farm residency is residency outside the area zoned as city limits and usually implies involvement in agriculture; nonfarm residency is residence within that zoned area.

q_0081.stem: How does the chapter characterize the relationship between rural and urban lifestyles?
options: They are opposing lifestyles with a clear dividing line
A continuum, from remote farm through village, town, and large metro area
Defined entirely by income level
Defined entirely by racial composition
q_0081.rationale: Rural and urban are not opposing lifestyles but a continuum: remote farm to village/small town to larger town/city to large metro area with a core inner city.

q_0082.stem: What is the "doughnut effect" as described in the chapter?
options: Rural residents moving into dense urban cores
A population shift from highly populated urban areas to outlying suburbs and less-populated regions
The concentration of health services in a metro area's center
A pattern of farm closures surrounding small towns
q_0082.rationale: The doughnut effect is the recent population shift from urban to less-populated regions, accelerated in 2020 as urban residents relocated during COVID-19.

q_0083.stem: Which statements about rural population characteristics are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Whites comprise about 80% of the rural population vs. 58% of urban
Rural communities have a higher proportion of residents younger than 18 and older than 65
Rural residents are more likely to have private insurance than urban residents
The "graying" of rural areas is partly due to retirees choosing rural areas
q_0083.rationale: Whites make up about 80% of the rural population versus 58% urban; rural communities skew younger-than-18 and older-than-65; retirees choosing rural areas for scenic beauty and pace of life contribute to the graying of rural populations.
q_0083.trap: Rural families are less likely to have private insurance and more likely to be uninsured or on public assistance — the opposite of option C.

q_0084.stem: Which factors explain why "working poor" families are more common in rural settings? Select all that apply.
options: High proportion of self-employment in family businesses like ranching or farming
Employment in small enterprises where insurance is not an employee benefit
Part-time or seasonal work without health insurance benefits
Income levels that qualify the family for public insurance
q_0084.rationale: The working poor are employed but cannot afford private insurance, and their income disqualifies them from public insurance. Rural settings drive this through self-employment in family businesses, small enterprises, and part-time or seasonal work without insurance benefits.
q_0084.trap: Working poor families are disqualified from public insurance by their income, not qualified for it.

q_0085.stem: According to the Rural Health Information Hub, which are named social determinants that are barriers to accessing rural care? Select all that apply.
options: Higher poverty rates
Low health literacy levels
Lower population densities limiting program economies of scale
Surplus of affordable, reliable transportation options
q_0085.rationale: The nine named barriers include higher poverty rates, low health literacy, linguistic and educational disparities, limited affordable or reliable transportation, unpredictable work hours, lower population densities, resource availability, and lack of access to healthy foods and physical activity.
q_0085.trap: Transportation is limited, not surplus, in rural areas — reverse of option D.

q_0086.stem: Box 24.2 describes several characteristics of rural life. Which are among them? Select all that apply.
options: Lack of anonymity
Preference for interacting with locals (insiders)
Mistrust of newcomers (outsiders)
Predominance of large industries over small family enterprises
q_0086.rationale: Box 24.2 names lack of anonymity, preference for interacting with insiders, and mistrust of outsiders as characteristic of rural life, along with small family enterprises rather than large industries. ---

q_0087.stem: Compared to urban adults, rural adults are more likely to do which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: Smoke
Report higher rates of alcohol use
Have more chronic health conditions
Wear seat belts
q_0087.rationale: Rural adults are more likely to smoke, report higher alcohol use, and have more chronic health conditions and mobility limitations.
q_0087.trap: Rural adults are less likely to wear seat belts, not more — that belongs on the "less likely" list along with physical activity, blood pressure checks, and cancer screenings.

q_0088.stem: Which statement correctly describes usual source of care patterns?
options: Urban adults are more likely than rural adults to identify a particular provider as their usual source of care
Rural adults are more likely than urban adults to identify a particular provider as their usual source of care
Neither group shows a difference in usual source of care
Rural adults are more likely to see a medical specialist as their usual provider
q_0088.rationale: Rural adults are more likely than urban adults to identify a particular medical provider as their usual source of care, most often a general practitioner or APRN. Urban adults are more likely to see a medical specialist.

q_0089.stem: Which figures correctly describe provider maldistribution between rural and urban areas?
options: Primary care physicians: 39.8 per 100,000 rural vs. 53.3 per 100,000 urban
Specialty physicians: 30 per 100,000 rural vs. 263 per 100,000 urban
Both A and B are accurate
Rural areas actually have more specialty physicians per capita
q_0089.rationale: Rural areas have 39.8 primary care physicians and 30 specialty physicians per 100,000, versus 53.3 and 263 respectively in urban areas — a much larger gap in specialty care than primary care.

q_0090.stem: Which statements about injury and accident risk in rural areas are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: More than 50% of vehicle crash-related fatalities occur in rural areas
There is an additional 22% risk of injury-related deaths in rural areas
Guns may be more readily found in rural vs. urban homes
Rural areas have lower rates of unintentional injury deaths than fringe metro counties
q_0090.rationale: More than half of vehicle crash fatalities occur in rural areas, with an additional 22% risk of injury-related death, and guns are more commonly found in rural homes due to distance from town and animal-related danger.
q_0090.trap: Box 24.3 shows the most rural counties have the HIGHEST death rates for unintentional and motor vehicle traffic injuries — the opposite of option D, which describes fringe metro counties.

q_0091.stem: Per Box 24.3, residents of the most rural counties (compared to fringe counties near large metro areas) have which outcomes? Select all that apply.
options: Highest death rates for children and young adults
Highest death rates among adults for ischemic heart disease and suicide
Fewest physician specialists and dentists per capita
Lowest percent without health insurance
q_0091.rationale: The most rural counties have the highest death rates for children/young adults and for ischemic heart disease/suicide among adults, and the fewest specialists and dentists per capita.
q_0091.trap: Fringe counties near large metro areas have the lowest percent without insurance — the most rural counties have the highest percent uninsured, not the lowest.

q_0092.stem: Which populations are named as particularly at risk for higher infant and maternal morbidity in rural areas? Select all that apply.
options: Women who live on or near Indian reservations
Migrant workers
Women of African American descent
Women in fringe counties near large metro areas
q_0092.rationale: Rural populations overall have higher infant and maternal morbidity, especially in counties designated as HPSAs; particularly at-risk groups named are women near Indian reservations, migrant workers, and women of African American descent.

q_0093.stem: Why is the incidence of rural sexual assault difficult to document, and what is the actual rate believed to be?
options: It's rarely reported because rates are genuinely lower in rural areas
Documentation is hard due to isolation and familiarity, but the rate is thought to be higher than in urban areas
It's well-documented and confirmed to be lower than urban rates
Reporting rates are identical to urban areas
q_0093.rationale: Incidence is hard to document because of rural isolation and the higher likelihood that the person assaulted knows people in the community; the rate is thought to be higher than in urban areas, not lower.
q_0093.trap: Under-documentation is the reason the rate looks lower on paper — it is not evidence that the actual rate is lower. Confidentiality concerns, familiarity with the person receiving the report, and family perpetrators all suppress reporting.

q_0094.stem: Which statement correctly compares usual providers for children in rural vs. urban settings?
options: Urban children are less likely to have a usual provider but more likely to see a pediatrician when ill
Rural children are less likely to have a usual provider
Urban children are more likely to see a general practitioner as their regular caregiver
There is no difference between rural and urban children's usual providers
q_0094.rationale: Urban children are less likely to have a usual provider but more likely to see a pediatrician when ill; rural adults and children are more likely to have a general practitioner as their regular caregiver.

q_0095.stem: Why are school nurses scarce in frontier and rural areas? Select all that apply.
options: A shortage of health care professionals
Fewer taxpayers, meaning less income to support school nurses
State laws prohibiting school nursing positions in rural districts
Federal restrictions on rural school funding
q_0095.rationale: The two named reasons are a shortage of health care professionals and fewer taxpayers providing less income to support school nurse positions. Workarounds include counties sharing a "district" health nurse or contracting with an urban agency.

q_0096.stem: Which statement best describes the pattern of mental health care-seeking among rural residents?
options: Rural residents seek care early, before symptoms escalate
Rural residents delay seeking care for emotional problems until an emergency or crisis arises
Rural residents seek mental health care at the same rate as urban residents
Rural residents primarily use telehealth for mental health concerns
q_0096.rationale: Rural residents delay seeking care for emotional problems until an emergency or crisis arises, even when services are available and accessible.

q_0097.stem: What mechanism does the chapter describe for underreporting of domestic violence and substance abuse in small rural communities?
options: Formal reporting systems are unavailable
When people are related or know each other well, they are less likely to report, and destructive coping behaviors may become accepted as usual for a particular family
Rural law enforcement actively discourages reporting
Substance abuse is rare in rural communities, reducing the need to report
q_0097.rationale: Familiarity reduces reporting likelihood, and in small, tight-knit communities destructive coping behaviors can come to be accepted as usual occurrences for a particular family.

q_0098.stem: Which factors are named as making rural Americans more vulnerable during COVID-19? Select all that apply.
options: Higher proportion of elderly residents
Higher smoking rates
Lower insurance coverage
Surplus hospital capacity and funding
q_0098.rationale: Rural Americans were more vulnerable due to a higher proportion of elderly residents, higher smoking rates, prevalence of certain chronic diseases, and lower insurance coverage. Nearly half of rural hospitals operate in a financial deficit, the opposite of surplus capacity. ---

q_0099.stem: Which four industries does OSHA identify as high-risk and predominantly rural?
options: Forestry, mining, marine-related fields, agriculture
Construction, manufacturing, transportation, agriculture
Forestry, retail, agriculture, hospitality
Mining, healthcare, agriculture, education
q_0099.rationale: The four OSHA-identified high-risk industries in predominantly rural environments are forestry, mining, marine-related fields, and agriculture.

q_0100.stem: Which statement correctly describes the regulatory status of small farms and ranches?
options: They fall fully under OSHA guidelines like other workplaces
Small enterprises with few employees do not fall under OSHA guidelines, and are also not covered by workers' compensation
They are covered by workers' compensation but not OSHA
They are covered by OSHA but not workers' compensation
q_0100.rationale: Small enterprises with a small number of employees do not fall under OSHA guidelines, so safety standards are not enforceable on most farms and ranches, and small businesses such as farms are not covered under workers' compensation insurance.
q_0100.trap: This is counterintuitive and therefore testable — farms and ranches are among the most dangerous workplaces, yet they escape both OSHA coverage and workers' compensation. Any option implying standard occupational safety law protects farmworkers is wrong.

q_0101.stem: Which are among the six most common health issues for farmworkers (NCFH, 2018b)? Select all that apply.
options: Pesticide exposure
Skin disorders
Musculoskeletal injuries
Cardiovascular disease
q_0101.rationale: The six most common health issues named are pesticide exposure, skin disorders, infectious diseases, musculoskeletal injuries, respiratory illnesses, and hearing and vision disorders. Cardiovascular disease is not among the six named.

q_0102.stem: A farmworker's child develops pesticide-related symptoms despite never entering the fields. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Airborne pesticide has no effect on children
The worker's clothing and dwelling can be a source of cross-contamination, along with drift and unwashed hands
Children are immune to organophosphate exposure
This can only occur through direct field exposure
q_0102.rationale: The farmworker's clothing and dwelling can be a major source of cross-contamination for both the worker and the family; entire families are at risk from drift, unwashed hands, and contaminated clothes brought home.

q_0103.stem: What is the Agricultural Worker Protection Standard (WPS), and when were its most recent EPA revisions implemented?
options: 1962; established migrant health centers
January 2017; restrictions on age of workers handling pesticides, training, and protective practices
1990; established OSHA field sanitation standards
2012; ACOG recommendation on LARC use
q_0103.rationale: The Agricultural Worker Protection Standard's EPA revisions were implemented in January 2017, restricting the age of workers who handle pesticides and mandating worker training and other protective practices.

q_0104.stem: Which are mild symptoms of pesticide poisoning, as distinguished from severe symptoms? Select all that apply.
options: Headache and dizziness
Eye irritation
Convulsions
Inability to breathe
q_0104.rationale: Mild symptoms include headache, fatigue, dizziness, nervousness, perspiration, loss of appetite, thirst, and eye/nose/throat irritation. Convulsions and inability to breathe are severe symptoms, along with fever, intense thirst, vomiting, muscle twitches, and unconsciousness.

q_0105.stem: Why does heat stress compound pesticide risk for farmworkers?
options: Heat has no relationship to pesticide absorption
Pesticides are more readily absorbed through hot, sweaty skin than through cool skin
Heat exposure reduces the amount of pesticide applied
Sweating washes pesticide residue away before it can be absorbed
q_0105.rationale: Pesticides are more readily absorbed through hot, sweaty skin than through cool skin, adding danger on top of the heat exhaustion symptoms themselves (heavy sweating, cold/pale/clammy skin, fast weak pulse, nausea, fainting).

q_0106.subtopic: levels of prevention for pesticide exposure
q_0106.stem: Per the textbook's Levels of Prevention box for rural health, which intervention represents secondary prevention for pesticide exposure?
options: Teaching workers how to reduce exposure
Conducting urine testing for pesticide exposure
Initiating treatment for nausea and skin irritation
Providing personal protective equipment during training
q_0106.rationale: The textbook specifically names urine testing as the secondary prevention intervention — screening to detect exposure that has already occurred, not yet symptomatic disease.
q_0106.trap: The textbook is unusually specific here — it names urine testing rather than blood work or general physical assessment. If an option offers a different screening modality, it does not match the source.

q_0107.subtopic: levels of prevention for pesticide exposure
q_0107.stem: A community health nurse initiates treatment for a farmworker's pesticide-related nausea and skin irritation. This represents which level of prevention?
options: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
Quaternary
q_0107.rationale: Per the textbook's Levels of Prevention box, initiating treatment for symptoms of pesticide exposure is tertiary prevention — managing an already-occurring condition. ---

q_0108.stem: A rural county has no hospital and no physicians practicing within 60 miles. Which barrier to care does this best illustrate?
options: Acceptability
Affordability
Availability
Accessibility
q_0108.rationale: Availability means health services exist and have the necessary personnel; sparseness of population limits the number and array of services in a region, which is exactly what an absent hospital and no nearby physicians describes.

q_0109.stem: A rural resident has a nearby clinic and can afford the visit, but lacks a car and there is no public transportation to reach it. Which barrier does this best illustrate?
options: Availability
Accessibility
Affordability
Acceptability
q_0109.rationale: Accessibility means a person has logistical access to needed services as well as the ability to purchase them; the described scenario is a logistical/transportation barrier.

q_0110.stem: A clinic exists and is reachable, but its services are not offered in a manner congruent with the community's cultural values, partly due to the urban orientation of health professionals. Which barrier does this best illustrate?
options: Availability
Accessibility
Affordability
Acceptability
q_0110.rationale: Acceptability means a service is appropriate and offered in a manner congruent with the values of a target population, hampered by both patient cultural preference and the urban orientation of health professions.

q_0111.stem: Which are named barriers to health care in rural areas per Box 24.4? Select all that apply.
options: Great distances to obtain services
Inequitable reimbursement policies for providers
Inadequate provider attitudes and understanding about rural populations
Surplus of publicly funded entitlement programs
q_0111.rationale: Box 24.4 names distance, transportation gaps, inequitable reimbursement, unpredictable weather, inability to pay, lack of know-how to procure entitlements, inadequate provider attitudes, and language and cultural barriers — not a surplus of entitlement programs.

q_0112.stem: What does the chapter say results from a demeaning provider attitude or insensitivity about rural lifestyle?
options: It has no measurable effect on the patient relationship
It generates mistrust, causing rural patients to view professionals as outsiders to the community
It only affects patients who are new to the area
It improves compliance because patients respect authority
q_0112.rationale: A demeaning attitude or insensitivity about rural lifestyle generates mistrust, causing rural patients to view professionals as outsiders to the community. Conversely, some rural providers report professional isolation and lack of community acceptance. ---

q_0113.stem: A farmworker travels to do agricultural work and cannot return to a permanent residence within the same day. How is this worker classified?
options: Seasonal farmworker
Migrant farmworker
Undocumented immigrant
Non-core resident
q_0113.rationale: A migrant farmworker is a seasonal farmworker who must travel to do farm work and is unable to return to a permanent residence within the same day.
q_0113.trap: This is the highest-probability confusable pair in the chapter. The discriminator is travel and same-day return, not the seasonality of the work — both migrant and seasonal workers do seasonal work. Migrant = travels, can't return home same day. Seasonal = returns to a permanent residence.

q_0114.stem: A farmworker returns home each night to a permanent residence and works in agriculture only part of the year, never working year-round exclusively in agriculture. How is this worker classified?
options: Migrant farmworker
Seasonal farmworker
Frontier resident
Documented immigrant
q_0114.rationale: A seasonal farmworker returns to a permanent residence, works in agriculture seasonally, and does not work year-round exclusively in agriculture.

q_0115.stem: Which statements about migrant and seasonal farmworker (MSFW) demographics are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: USDA estimated 1.0 to 2.7 million MSFWs in the United States
70.7% of MSFWs are foreign born, most commonly from Mexico
The majority of MSFWs are hired through labor contractors rather than directly
Roughly 28% reported being unable to speak English at all
q_0115.rationale: USDA estimated 1.0–2.7 million MSFWs; 70.7% are foreign born with 64.1% born in Mexico; 28% reported being unable to speak English at all.
q_0115.trap: 85% of farmworkers are hired directly, and only 15% are contract workers — the reverse of option C.

q_0116.stem: What are the three traditional migratory streams and their states of origin?
options: Eastern from New York, Midwestern from Illinois, Western from Oregon
Eastern from Florida, Midwestern from Texas, Western from California
Eastern from Georgia, Midwestern from Kansas, Western from Nevada
There are only two traditional streams, not three
q_0116.rationale: The three traditional migratory streams are Eastern originating in Florida, Midwestern originating in Texas, and Western originating in California. These streams are becoming less distinct as workers travel more widely.

q_0117.stem: Which factors does the textbook name as making MSFWs a "unique vulnerable population"? Select all that apply.
options: Mobility
Physical demands of their work
Social and geographic isolation
High rates of home ownership
q_0117.rationale: The textbook's own list is mobility, the physical demands of their work, social and often geographic isolation, language differences, and high rates of financial impoverishment — not home ownership.

q_0118.stem: Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, which farms are exempt from minimum wage requirements?
options: Farms with more than seven full-time workers
Farms with fewer than seven workers in a calendar quarter
All farms regardless of size
No farms are exempt from FLSA minimum wage
q_0118.rationale: Farms with fewer than seven workers in a calendar quarter are exempt from minimum wage under the FLSA; farmworkers are also not included in overtime pay protections regardless of farm size.

q_0119.stem: What does the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act require of contractors and employers? Select all that apply.
options: Disclose employment terms
Post worker protection information at the worksite
Ensure housing complies with federal and state safety standards
Provide employer-sponsored health insurance regardless of hours worked
q_0119.rationale: The Act requires disclosure of employment terms, posted worker protection information, itemized pay statements, and housing that meets safety standards. It does not mandate employer health insurance; the chapter separately notes many workers are excluded from ACA coverage due to the small-farm exemption and the 120-day seasonal exclusion.

q_0120.stem: Which signs suggest possible labor trafficking among farmworkers? Select all that apply.
options: Performing work duties in exchange for basic necessities rather than money
Identification documents held by the employer
Freedom to choose and change housing at will
Inability to freely choose where they live
q_0120.rationale: Signs include working for necessities instead of pay, an employer holding identification documents, and inability to freely choose housing — not freedom to change housing at will, which would be the opposite of a red flag.

q_0121.stem: A nursing assessment identifies a minor as a likely victim of labor trafficking. What is the correct nursing action?
options: Obtain the minor's permission before contacting authorities
Notify child protective services and law enforcement; the minor should not be left alone until services arrive
Wait until the minor turns 18 to involve authorities
Refer the case to the employer for internal resolution
q_0121.rationale: If a minor is identified, the nurse should notify child protective services and law enforcement, and the minor should not be left alone until services arrive.
q_0121.trap: Obtaining permission before contacting authorities applies to adult victims, not minors — for a minor, reporting is not optional and does not require the minor's consent first.

q_0122.stem: What is named as a common consequence of pesticide exposure combined with substandard migrant housing conditions? Select all that apply.
options: Tuberculosis
Gastroenteritis
Hepatitis
Improved sanitation compared to urban housing
q_0122.rationale: Poor and crowded residence contributes to tuberculosis, gastroenteritis, hepatitis, and lead exposure — housing is generally substandard, not improved compared to other settings. ---

q_0123.subtopic: TB, access barriers, and health problems
q_0123.stem: Why is tuberculosis treatment especially difficult to complete among migrant farmworkers?
options: TB medication is dispensed monthly, but adequate treatment requires 6 to 12 months, and workers who relocate must independently seek new services to continue treatment
Migrant workers are not susceptible to TB
TB medication does not require ongoing follow-up
Migrant health centers do not provide TB treatment
q_0123.rationale: Health departments dispense TB medications monthly, but adequate treatment requires 6 to 12 months; when workers move, they must independently seek out new health services, and incomplete treatment contributes to resistant TB.

q_0124.subtopic: TB, access barriers, and health problems
q_0124.stem: What is the purpose of the Migrant Clinicians Network (MCN) TB tracking program?
options: To deny services to workers with a TB history
To make previous provider information available to a farmworker's current provider, maintaining continuity of TB care
To replace the need for monthly medication dispensing
To track farmworkers for immigration enforcement purposes
q_0124.rationale: The MCN TB tracking program makes previous provider information available to a farmworker's current provider, maintaining continuity of TB care for a mobile population.

q_0125.subtopic: TB, access barriers, and health problems
q_0125.stem: Which factors limit adequate provision of health care services to migrant farmworkers? Select all that apply.
options: Health care records typically do not travel with families as they move
Services are often available only during work hours, meaning lost earnings to seek care
Undocumented workers are excluded from employer and individual insurance mandates
Medicaid eligibility follows workers seamlessly across state lines
q_0125.rationale: Records fragmenting, lost earnings from seeking care during work hours, and exclusion of undocumented workers from insurance mandates are all named barriers. Medicaid eligibility does NOT follow seamlessly — workers may lose benefits when relocating to a state with different eligibility standards.

q_0126.subtopic: TB, access barriers, and health problems
q_0126.stem: Which health problems are most often reported among migrant workers (NCFH, 2018a)? Select all that apply.
options: Overweight/obesity and hypertension
Diabetes mellitus
Otitis media and eustachian tube disorders
Osteoporosis
q_0126.rationale: Most often reported issues are overweight/obesity, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, otitis media and eustachian tube disorders, depression and other mood disorders, and substance abuse — osteoporosis is not named.

q_0127.subtopic: TB, access barriers, and health problems
q_0127.stem: What does the term "nervios" refer to in the context of migrant health?
options: A physical illness caused by pesticide exposure
A term used by some Western hemisphere Hispanics for increased susceptibility to mental stress and nervousness symptoms
A folk term for tuberculosis
A term describing chronic fatigue from fieldwork
q_0127.rationale: Nervios is a term used by some Western hemisphere Hispanics for increased susceptibility to mental stress and symptoms of nervousness; 22% of a California farmworker household survey reported it.

q_0128.subtopic: TB, access barriers, and health problems
q_0128.stem: Which statement about diabetes among the Latino farmworker population is accurate?
options: Prevalence is similar to the general US population
Prevalence is estimated three to five times greater than the general population, with higher rates of end-stage complications
Prevalence is lower than the general population due to diet
Diabetes is not tracked separately for this population
q_0128.rationale: Diabetes prevalence among the US Latino population is estimated three to five times greater than the general population, with CDC incidence of 8.4 per 1000 versus 5.7 per 1000 for non-Hispanic whites.

q_0129.subtopic: TB, access barriers, and health problems
q_0129.stem: Which HIV risk factors are named specifically for migrant farmworker populations? Select all that apply.
options: Sharing needles for common medications such as vitamins and antibiotics
Needle sharing through amateur tattooing
Isolation and separation from families
Routine access to comprehensive sex education
q_0129.rationale: Named risk factors include sharing needles for medications like vitamins and antibiotics, needle sharing through amateur tattooing, isolation from families, unprotected sexual activity, and limited education — not routine access to comprehensive sex education, which would be protective rather than a risk factor.

q_0130.stem: A nurse performs nutrition education at a migrant camp. Per Box 24.5's worked example, this represents which level of prevention?
options: Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
None of these — nutrition education is not a prevention activity
q_0130.rationale: Box 24.5's worked example classifies nutrition education as primary prevention, diabetes screening as secondary prevention, and a self-care educational program for those already diagnosed as tertiary prevention.

q_0131.stem: Which age ranges correctly match the two named programs for migrant children?
options: Migrant and Seasonal Head Start Program: 6 months to 5 years; Migrant Education Program: older than 5 years, a summer school program
Migrant and Seasonal Head Start Program: older than 5 years; Migrant Education Program: 6 months to 5 years
Both programs serve children 6 months to 5 years
Both programs serve children older than 5 years
q_0131.rationale: The Migrant and Seasonal Head Start Program serves children 6 months to 5 years, while the Migrant Education Program is a summer school program for children older than 5, currently offered in only 38 states.
q_0131.trap: The age ranges are easy to invert. Head Start = younger (6 months–5 years); Migrant Education = older (over 5, summer school).

q_0132.stem: Under FLSA child labor rules in agriculture, at what age may a child work any farm job at any time, including hazardous work with no restriction on hours?
options: 12 and older
16 and older
Federal law never permits hazardous agricultural work by minors
q_0132.rationale: Workers 16 and older may work any farm job at any time, including hazardous work, with no restrictions on hours. Federal law does not protect children from overworking or limit hours worked outside school in agriculture, unlike other industries.

q_0133.stem: What educational consequences are named for children of migrant farmworkers? Select all that apply.
options: Being too tired after working to do homework
Leaving school before the end of the term to travel with families
Attending three to five different schools each year
Consistently outperforming peers due to varied educational settings
q_0133.rationale: Named consequences include exhaustion after work interfering with homework, leaving school early and arriving late in the fall, and attending three to five different schools each year — not improved academic outcomes. ---
